title: AMD Stock Looks Poised to Revisit Its All-Time Highs

Advanced Micro Devices' (AMD) stock looks poised to revisit its all-time highs. The market has already bought into its growth story. Now, the next opportunity may lie in how much of that growth turns into profits. After a triple-digit gain in 2026, the stock has pulled back from its October record highs, but the fundamentals help explain much of that rally.

In its third-quarter earnings report, released on November 3, the Santa Clara, California-based chipmaker reported that its Data Center revenue nearly doubled, along with a great improvement in margins.

The most interesting part may still be ahead. With much greater visibility into 2027, I believe the market still underestimates the company's earnings growth potential. That's why I remain bullish, even with an already demanding valuation.

AMD's Data Center Growth Explains Much of the Rally

First, I think it's important to put AMD's remarkable triple-digit rally this year into context. I see two key metrics that have marked a turning point in the company's investment thesis: Data Center revenue growth and forward revenue growth.

Let's start by breaking down the first metric. Basically, the market has gone from viewing AMD as a central processing unit (CPU) manufacturer trying to gain ground in artificial intelligence (AI) graphics processing units (GPUs) to treating it as a potential second major AI infrastructure platform, behind Nvidia (NVDA).

The acceleration driven by AI demand really began to show up in AMD's results in 2026, something that wasn't nearly as pronounced in 2025. To be more specific, in the third quarter of 2025, AMD generated $4.34 billion in Data Center revenue, up 22% year-over-year. A year later, that revenue reached $8.55 billion, a 97% jump, driven by both EPYC processors, benefiting particularly from the growth of AI agents, and Instinct MI450 GPUs. As a result, Data Center now accounts for 64% of the company's total revenue, compared to less than 50% in the same period last year.

As if that weren't enough, this growth came with a considerable improvement in the segment's profitability. Data Center's operating margin rose from 25% to 34%. So, we're talking about a company whose core business has nearly doubled in size while its margins have expanded by an impressive 9 percentage points.

title: Bank of America resets AMD stock price target as Nvidia CEO exits
detail:
Bank of America resets AMD stock price target as Nvidia CEO exits
Moz Farooque, Celine Provini
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 12:13 PM PST 5 min read
NVDA
BAC
AMD
AVGO
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

On Nov. 12, when Nvidia (NVDA) confirmed that its CEO, Jensen Huang, had resigned, investors surprisingly didn't sell every AI chip stock.

In fact, Wall Street piled into Nvidia's biggest rivals, adding insult to injury. Nvidia stock shed 4.3% to $166.19 on Nov. 12, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) surged 5.9% to $585.30, and Broadcom (AVGO) gained 5.5%. 

Bank of America made a similar distinction in a note shared with me. Veteran analyst Vivek Arya bumped his AMD price target, cut Nvidia's, and kept a Buy rating on both.

But perhaps the more revealing number in Arya's analysis isn't the flashy new price target, but a massive new forecast for a market that tends to be overshadowed by AI accelerators.

Bank of America's $700 target starts with a different chip

Arya raised his AMD stock price target to $700 from $650 and slashed Nvidia's to $280 from $350. At the Nov. 12 close, AMD's new target implied 19.6% upside.

However, what has him reassessing his outlook on AMD is a substantial bump in his forecast for the server CPU market, which often gets overlooked amid AI GPU headlines.

He estimates the server CPU market could rise to $240 billion by 2030, up from $210 billion in his previous guidance. Interestingly, he expects AI agents to effectively drive that growth.

GPUs handle the heavy computation behind AI models, but CPUs handle work around those models, which means more AI activity drives demand for both kinds of chips.

Arya called AMD his top CPU pick, citing the breadth of its processor lineup, clock speeds, core and thread counts, and better visibility into supply. 

Speaking of processors, on Nov. 10, AMD announced general availability of its sixth-generation EPYC server processors, based on Zen 6, and said systems using them were already shipping. In fact, Microsoft Azure and Oracle had also confirmed plans to use the new chips.

AMD has already set a massive bar.

Its data-center sales skyrocketed 97% to $8.5 billion in Q3, with both EPYC CPUs and Instinct GPUs contributing. CEO Lisa Su told analysts on the earnings call that she expects the data-center CPU business to roughly double in 2027, according to Reuters. 

Looking ahead, AMD's Q4 outlook calls for $17 billion in companywide sales and a 55% adjusted gross margin, compared to 56% in Q3, a reminder that there's still plenty of work to be done on the margins side.

Bank of America lifts AMD's price target as Nvidia's CEO steps down.
KENT NISHIMURA / Getty Images
What AMD investors are paying for at $585

The new $700 target recovers $50 of the $70 Arya cut earlier in November. 

In that specific move, BofA has lifted its adjusted earnings estimates to $16.95 per share for 2027 and $26.14 per share for 2028, but has lowered the target from $720 to $650 as chip stock pricing multiples contracted.

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) stock is sinking, down 10.8% as of 1:20 a.m. ET on Friday, Nov. 13, as the chip sector sells off amid the developing scandal at rival Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA).

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) and the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) were down 0.8% and 1.3%, respectively.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Why AMD stock is falling after Jensen Huang's resignation

On Thursday, now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned, effective immediately, after the second revelation of an extramarital affair, this time with a direct report within his former company. The scandal goes well beyond the personal, however: the first alleged affair was with a suspected Chinese spy who was reportedly instrumental in funneling at least $7.5 billion of Nvidia chips into China.

Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

Initially, the news helped AMD's stock on bets that customers would shift their AI chip orders to Nvidia rivals, but on Friday, it seemed investors are more worried the scandal could represent a more fundamental risk to the industry.

Of course, AMD stock gained almost 50% in a week heading into today, so some of this decline is probably investors locking in some profits.

Why the Nvidia investigation could weigh on chip stocks

I think the effects of the Nvidia scandal may be longer lasting than many hope. The investigation has really just begun, and if Congress or federal regulators uncover evidence that Huang, or any other Nvidia officers, had knowledge of chips being diverted to China in violation of export controls, things could get rocky.
